zh.title: 波音737 MAX、747-8與787引擎鋸齒噴嘴　降噪成功卻付出燃油代價
zh.summary: 波音在737 MAX、747-8與787引擎噴嘴上採用的鋸齒狀「chevron」設計，成功降低機場噪音，卻在巡航全程造成阻力與推力損失；空中巴士從未跟進，波音自己也在777X上捨棄了這項設計。
body: 現代商用噴射引擎已是極為精密的工程結晶，更安靜、更省油、也更潔淨，但波音三款重要機型——737 MAX、747-8與787夢幻客機——卻搭載一項獨特設計，帶來幾乎沒有其他現代客機面臨的問題：鋸齒狀引擎排氣噴嘴「chevron」。噴嘴後緣的鋸齒狀圖案最初是為了降低噪音而設計，波音與奇異（GE）及美國國家航空暨太空總署（NASA）共同開發，以因應日益嚴格的機場噪音法規。波音先在787上商業導入此技術，再擴及747-8與737 MAX全系列；787不論搭載勞斯萊斯Trent 1000或奇異GEnx引擎皆採用chevron。

chevron的原理是讓引擎兩股排氣流更平緩地混合：渦輪風扇引擎同時排出高溫高速的核心氣流與較冷的旁通氣流，兩者交互作用產生的亂流是引擎噪音的主要來源；鋸齒邊緣產生可控渦流，使排氣流逐漸混合，降低排氣羽流的聲學強度，NASA在研發期間的研究證實，機場周邊可感知的引擎噪音確實下降。然而刻意製造的渦流不會在飛機離開機場後消失，混合過程在整個航程中持續進行，包括巡航階段；渦流輕微擾動排氣流、增加阻力並降低引擎效率與推力輸出。航空分析師佩特·霍恩費爾特（Petter Hörnfeldt）估計，chevron造成的推力損失約為0.5%，數字雖小，但在航空經濟學中，極小的效率損失亦具實質意義。

空中巴士從未在任何現代客機上採用此技術，而是依靠短艙聲學處理、先進風扇設計與高旁通比引擎降噪；波音的chevron專利最初使競爭對手無法商業使用該設計，專利保護至2021年屆滿，但專利到期後空中巴士仍無興趣，A350總工程師道吉·杭特（Dougie Hunter）公開表示，空中巴士認為chevron的降噪效益不足以抵銷其比油耗損失。波音自己也在最新旗艦777X上完全捨棄chevron，改與奇異開發以陶瓷基複合材料（CMC）打造的全新噴嘴結構，GE9X總專案工程師泰瑞·比茲霍德（Terry Beezhold）表示，新噴嘴在噪音表現相當的同時阻力更低、重量更輕，整體約比舊設計輕20%。787是例外：由於引擎外部噪音大幅降低，波音得以減少機身隔音材料達600磅（約272公斤），重量節省部分抵銷了chevron的性能損失。

en.title: How the Boeing 737 MAX, 747-8 and 787 Dreamliner's engines create problems no other modern jet faces
en.summary: The serrated chevron nozzles on the Boeing 737 MAX, 747-8 and 787 engines cut airport noise but impose drag and thrust losses through every phase of flight; Airbus never adopted them, and Boeing itself abandoned the design on the 777X.
body: Modern commercial jet engines are among the most refined pieces of engineering ever developed: quieter, more fuel-efficient and dramatically cleaner than earlier generations. Yet three of Boeing's most important aircraft families, the Boeing 737 MAX, 747-8 and 787 Dreamliner, carry an unusual design feature that introduces a problem almost no competing modern jet faces: serrated engine exhaust nozzles known as chevrons. The distinctive sawtooth patterns on the rear edges of the engine nacelles were designed primarily to reduce noise. Boeing developed the concept alongside General Electric and NASA as airlines faced increasingly strict airport noise regulations. Boeing introduced the technology commercially on the 787 before expanding it to the 747-8 and the 737 MAX family; every 787 engine variant uses chevrons, whether powered by Rolls-Royce Trent 1000s or General Electric GEnx engines.

Chevrons work by mixing the engine's two exhaust flows more gradually. Modern turbofans produce a hot, high-velocity core stream and a cooler bypass airflow, and the interaction between the two creates turbulence, a major source of jet engine noise. The serrated edges generate controlled vortices that blend the streams together, lowering the acoustic intensity of the exhaust plume; NASA research during development confirmed measurable reductions in perceived engine noise around airports. But the vortices do not disappear once the aircraft leaves the airport environment: the mixing continues throughout the entire flight, including cruise, slightly disrupting exhaust flow, increasing drag and marginally lowering thrust. Aviation analyst Petter Hörnfeldt, known through Mentour Pilot, has estimated the thrust penalty at approximately 0.5%; while the figure appears small, aviation economics are built around extremely thin performance margins.

Airbus never adopted the technology on any competing modern aircraft program, relying instead on nacelle acoustic treatments, advanced fan designs and high bypass ratio engines. Boeing's patented chevron design initially prevented competitors from using the concept commercially, and that patent protection remained in place until 2021; even after it expired, Airbus showed no interest. A350 Chief Engineer Dougie Hunter publicly explained that Airbus found no compelling advantage in the technology, determining that chevrons did not provide sufficient noise benefits to justify the associated specific fuel consumption penalty. Boeing itself abandoned chevrons entirely for the 777X and its GE9X engines, developing a different nozzle architecture using ceramic matrix composites; GE9X Chief Project Engineer Terry Beezhold explained that the new nozzle provides equivalent cabin and community noise levels with lower drag and lighter construction, reportedly around 20% lighter than older designs. The trade-off was more favourable on the 787, where quieter engines let Boeing eliminate up to 600 pounds, or roughly 272 kilograms, of acoustic insulation, partly offsetting the performance penalty.
